This Is Oblio, a Warm and Functional Bus Home DIYed by the "Grandmaster Skoolie Builder" Himself
22 photos
Photo: Mobile Dwellings/YouTube screenshot
If you're a bus lifer, a DIYer in the process of building your own school bus home, or simply a fan of skoolie conversions, you’ve probably heard of Chuck Cassady. The man is a legend in the world of bus living. Known to many as the Grandmaster Skoolie Builder, he has spent nearly a decade honing his skills, helping others build their mobile homes, and sharing what he has learned through online videos.
Cassady ran a bus conversion company for almost a decade, appeared on several TV shows, and published around 200 YouTube videos to help people complete their own DIY skoolie projects. Today, I’m going to take a closer look at the second bus home he built for himself from scratch, a gorgeous build he christened Oblio.
Based on a decommissioned school bus he bought in May 2021, Oblio showcases Chuck’s craftsmanship, technical knowledge, and attention to detail, combining practical design with a livable layout, beautiful finishes, and reliable systems for off-grid living.
As Chuck himself confesses in the video attached below, his journey into skoolie life began out of necessity in 2015. He was in college back then and he couldn’t afford rent, so he decided to live in his first bus, which he lovingly called Queen of Peace. He knew little about building at the time, but he was willing to learn and the experience helped him gain new skills. Things eventually evolved into a skoolie building business, and then he also started a YouTube channel to share all the knowledge he has gained along the way.
Photo: Mobile Dwellings/YouTube screenshot Oblio is the second bus he builds for himself. It’s based on a 1996 International chassis fitted with a Thomas school bus body and measures 27.5 feet (8.4 meters) long. It’s way shorter than Chuck’s previous 38-foot (11.5-meter) bus conversion, but what draw him in was the engine. The school district had installed a new Cummins engine in 2018, shortly before the bus left service, and it’s the kind of engine you typically find in larger 40-foot (12.2-meter) school buses. And the best part, it only had about 30,000 miles (48,280 km) on it when he purchased it.
He still made a few modifications to the mechanical part, like installing a larger radiator, changing the transmission, and replacing every hose and belt, before beginning the actual conversion process.
To make it more comfortable to live in full time, Chuck raised the roof by 12 inches (30 cm), which resulted in more headroom inside, and replaced the original school bus windows with RV windows. He also painted the bus’s exterior is a pleasant olive green shade that allows it to blend in with natural environments.
Photo: Mobile Dwellings/YouTube screenshot He also built three storage bays that carry his tools, outdoor equipment, and personal belongings, and added as many solar panels as he could fit on the roof to support off-grid living. At the rear of the bus, the doors open to reveal a huge garage area that holds a 125-gallon (473-liter) freshwater tank, the water heater, and the power system components.
But Chuck’s excellent craftsmanship and efficient use of space are more noticeable inside Oblio, where he created an open living space with a front lounge, a dinette, a central kitchen, a separate bathroom, and a rear bedroom. Since the school bus is shorter, he had to fit everything inside a compact floor plan, but he definitely made every inch count. On top of that, the use of warm wood finishes, curved cabinetry, and discreet lighting gives it a warm, cozy feel.
The choice of materials played an important role in how welcoming the interior feels. Cedar closet liner was used on the curved ceiling, the countertops are made from Richlite, a durable material made from compressed paper, and Marmoleum covers the floor. Marmoleum is also a durable, waterproof material made from 97% natural materials, including crushed limestone, linseed oil, wood flour, and jute. Oak details add even more warmth, and the rounded edges also soften the interior.
Photo: Mobile Dwellings/YouTube screenshot At the front of the bus, Chuck installed a new driver’s seat but still has to redo the dash area. But as you step into the actual habitat, the first area is the lounge, which is also his office, dining space, and everyday living area. He furnished it with a custom sofa and a separate dinette for two.
To help maintain an organized, uncluttered interior, he had to come up with clever storage solutions, so upper shelves run along both sides of the interior, the dinette is raised to create storage underneath, the seating benches have built-in drawers, and the table also has a small slide-out junk drawer underneath. Even the sofa has hidden storage behind its cushions.
Photo: Mobile Dwellings/YouTube screenshot Moving further into the bus, we discover the kitchen, which features a long Richlite countertop, walnut cabinet fronts, and a tiled backsplash finished with epoxy grout. He equipped the cooking area with an induction cooktop, an oven, and a large undercounter marine-style refrigerator. A pull-out pantry and numerous drawers provide plenty of space for pots, pottery, utensils, and supplies. A separate cabinet integrates a stainless-steel undermount sink with a foot-pedal faucet.
Despite the bus’s modest dimensions, Chuck wanted a proper bathroom, so he built an elongated space with a large shower, a custom vanity with curved edges, an asymmetrical backlit mirror, and a composting toilet. The whole bathroom has tile walls, while the exterior curved wall is decorated with a flowery wallpaper.
The rear of the skoolie is Chuck’s bedroom. It features a raised fixed bed flanked by two opening windows and with a curved illuminted shelf surrounding it. A pair of storage stairs makes climbing into bed easier, and beside the bed, there is a wardrobe with a nifty tray-like nightstand area above it, perfect for keeping books, remote controls, gadgets, and other knick-knacks.
Photo: Mobile Dwellings/YouTube screenshot According to Chuck, Oblio was built to support an off-grid lifestyle, though the power system capacity is not mentioned. The main idea, however, is that this skoolie gives him the freedom to travel and help other people with their own projects.
In terms of costs, the bus itself was $5,500, and though Chuck didn’t keep a record of everything he purchased for the build, he estimates he spent about $60,000 on materials. He also put between 800 to 1,000 work hours into the build.
